projects.title: Clpr
projects.summary: Find a Twitch clip again by creator, topic, or tag. I built the Go API, React interface, moderation tools, and hybrid search, and operate the public deployment.
projects.description: Clpr lets a community find, organize, discuss, and share Twitch clips. I built the Go API, React web client, PostgreSQL model, moderation tools, and hybrid search pipeline, alongside container releases and production operations. The responsive web app is available today; native mobile apps are planned.
projects.problem: A Twitch clip is easy to make and hard to find a week later. Viewers had no dependable place to vote on clips, organize them, talk about them, or search for one they half remember.
highlights: Built clip discovery, playlists, voting, discussions, and moderation around one Go API and responsive React client.
Designed hybrid lexical and semantic retrieval so exact clip metadata and conversational queries can use different relevance signals.
Operate the public clpr.tv deployment from a tested, tagged release with documented verification and rollback paths.
architecture: The React client uses a versioned Go API for discovery, accounts, playlists, and moderation. PostgreSQL owns the durable data; client behavior stays separate from retrieval and background processing.
Clip titles and tags benefit from exact matching, while conversational queries need semantic retrieval. I combined BM25 and vector search so each path can be evaluated and fail independently.

PostgreSQL remains the system of record, while Redis handles sessions and caching and OpenSearch serves retrieval. Keeping those responsibilities separate improves recovery, at the cost of explicit synchronization and health checks.
lessons: A hybrid search stack adds operational cost, so its lexical and semantic paths need independent failure handling and measurable relevance tests.
A versioned API keeps interface changes separate from retrieval and moderation behavior, but requires explicit contract checks.

projects.title: Subcorp
projects.summary: A self-hosted platform where six named agents propose, debate, and run missions through real-time chat and sandboxed tools.
projects.description: Six named agents use Subcorp to propose work, debate approaches, run missions, and talk through the real-time Sanctum interface. Each agent has a distinct identity and access boundary. The app combines Next.js, React, PostgreSQL with pgvector, WebSockets, queued workflows, and a sandbox for bash, file I/O, web search, and memory retrieval.
projects.problem: Six agents sharing tools and a chat room need clear identities, ordered messages, and strict access boundaries. Without them, simultaneous actions conflict and tool access becomes unsafe.
highlights: Deployed a live system where six agents propose, debate, and run missions with limited human intervention.
Built a real-time Sanctum chat interface with WebSocket-driven @mention routing, whisper channels, and structured roundtable conversation modes.
Designed a sandboxed toolbox container giving agents access to bash, Python, Node.js, web search, file I/O, and semantic memory, isolated from the host system.
architecture: The app is Next.js 16 and React 19. PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector holds 45 tables, including the agents' semantic memory, and the OpenRouter SDK handles model calls.
A WebSocket layer carries agent-to-agent and agent-to-user messages, with structured routing, @mention parsing and private whispers.
Agents run bash, Python and Node.js, search the web and read and write files inside a Docker container that is network-isolated from the host and resource-limited.
lessons: The same model behaves very differently once it has a distinct identity, relationships with the other agents and its own tool permissions. Those settings mattered as much as which model I picked.
Ordering messages between six agents was the hard part. Race conditions between agents proposing actions at the same moment were the hardest bugs I had to debug.

projects.coreMechanism: Autonomous multi-agent orchestration loop with bounded delegation
projects.shippedOutcome: Self-hosted six-agent mission and chat platform

projects.title: HasanAra
projects.summary: Search long broadcasts and open a result at the second it was spoken. I built the archive interface and the shared Python transcription and search system behind it. Automatic transcripts need checking against the recording.
projects.description: HasanAra is a broadcast archive running on Rekolekt, the shared headless transcription and search backend. I built the React archive interface and the Python/FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL job model, GPU transcription workers, and release path. The archive frontend and configuration now live separately from the reusable core. Transcripts are automatic and sometimes wrong; verify quotations against the source recording.
projects.problem: Hundreds of hours of long-form video hold statements, recurring themes and research material that nobody can realistically find by scrubbing through playback.
highlights: Built a timestamped transcript search interface with surrounding context, passage links, saved moments, and exports.
Built a tagging pipeline that extracts entities, recurring topics and themes from transcripts so results can be filtered by them.
Built a GPU transcription and enrichment pipeline with queue-backed workers, retryable ingestion, and durable PostgreSQL job state.
Set up an explicit API contract, browser tests, health checks and release automation.
architecture: Because transcription and NLP enrichment jobs must survive worker restarts, I keep job and application state together in PostgreSQL and use SKIP LOCKED claims. This avoids a separate queue service but requires stuck-job recovery and explicit retries.

PostgreSQL owns durable transcript, automated tag hierarchies, and account data, while OpenSearch serves cross-channel full-text retrieval and faceted tag filtering. Export pipelines produce SRT, VTT, and PDF without making the search index authoritative.

Rekolekt owns the API and GPU workers; HasanAra owns the archive frontend and deployment profile. Separating them lets archives share backend improvements while retaining their own source configuration and interface.
lessons: A PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED queue keeps job state and application state in one transactional system, but requires explicit retry and stuck-job recovery behavior.
Giving an archive its own name on shared software means the naming, authentication, documentation and release metadata all have to change together. A visual rename alone is not enough.

projects.title: Prichal
projects.summary: Managed hosting for AT Protocol account servers, so a Bluesky user can have a server of their own without running it. I built the Go control plane, the restricted host agent, the certificate and restore operators, and the React dashboard. It is a private preview with no public sign-up.
projects.description: Every Bluesky account lives on a personal data server (PDS). Prichal runs each customer's PDS in its own container on a managed host and handles the upkeep. I built the Go API and River job worker on PostgreSQL, a node agent that runs only a fixed set of operations over mutual TLS, Ansible-provisioned KVM guests, hourly certificate renewal with automatic rollback, and encrypted checkpoints that restore into an isolated guest. A closed staging PDS and the management dashboard are live behind sign-in. Public sign-up, accounts and production provisioning are not done yet.
projects.problem: Leaving Bluesky's own servers means running a PDS yourself: a machine, certificates, backups and upgrades. Most people who want their account on their own server will not do that work.
highlights: Kept the public API away from Docker sockets and fleet credentials. A node agent accepts only defined operations on pinned images over mutual TLS.
Built hourly certificate renewal that keeps private keys inside each guest, sends only signing requests over SSH, and rolls back automatically. A deliberately failed run proved the rollback.
Restored encrypted checkpoints into a network-restricted guest and confirmed the clone could not reach the identity directory, so a restore cannot publish a duplicate account identity.
architecture: Customer PDS containers share managed hosts instead of getting a VM each. Each PDS keeps its own SQLite data, separate from the management database. That keeps hosting affordable, and the product copy promises container isolation, not a dedicated machine.

Provisioning, renewal and recovery run as River jobs in PostgreSQL, so enqueueing is transactional and retries are bounded. Effects outside the database still have to be idempotent, and after a database restore the worker reconciles live host inventory before it processes recovered jobs.

Hosts run a separate agent that the API reaches over mutual TLS. Customers cannot pass shell commands, images, Compose files or volume paths through it. This costs an extra service and its certificate operations, but a compromised API cannot run arbitrary containers.
lessons: SSH connection sharing hid a dead tunnel: a tunnel could exit successfully while it depended on a shared master connection. The supervised units now disable sharing, and a restart test is what exposed it.
Passing builds do not prove an exit gate. Each milestone in the roadmap stays open until a live check covers it, which is why sign-up is still listed as unqualified.
projects.coreMechanism: Restricted mTLS node agent with River jobs, certificate rollback and isolated restore drills
projects.shippedOutcome: Private preview with a closed staging PDS, dashboard sign-in and tested recovery

projects.title: Undertow
projects.summary: Layer visuals, artwork, and timed lyrics around a track, then export video in the browser. I built the React editor and WebCodecs rendering pipeline; codec support depends on the browser and hardware.
projects.description: Undertow lays out each layer separately for 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1 and encodes the video in the browser with WebCodecs. I built the React and Zustand editor, the Butterchurn Milkdrop layer, lyric timing from LRC, SRT and VTT, and the export pipeline. A Hono API and a headless Chrome worker render the same page server-side for cloud renders, which are still in testing. Paid plans are off.
projects.problem: A track posted as a video needs something to look at. Building a visualizer usually means learning a video editor. Undertow puts the layers in a browser editor and renders the video on the musician's own computer.
highlights: Export advances time at a fixed frame rate and decodes video layers to the exact frame, so the output does not depend on how fast the machine renders.

Copies canvas frames to the CPU before encoding: about 6 ms per 1080p frame against about 75 ms for passing the canvas directly, measured in Chrome on Apple silicon. A fallback covers devices where the copy fails.
Writes the MP4 in seekable Blob chunks, so long exports do not need a file-sized buffer in memory.
architecture: The cloud worker loads the same render page in headless Chrome and calls the same export function. There is no second renderer to keep in sync. Milkdrop then runs on software WebGL, which is much slower than a GPU.
The exporter tries H.264, then HEVC, VP9 and AV1 for video, and AAC then Opus for audio. If no audio encoder is available, the export is silent and the dialog says so instead of failing.
Milkdrop preset choices are seeded so the preview and the export pick the same presets, although Milkdrop output is not bit-identical between runs.
lessons: The first CI runs exposed assumptions the local setup hid: service-name DNS missing on the runner's default Docker bridge, and a fixture reset racing an asynchronous usage insert.
Copy has to follow what is switched on. While live billing is off, the editor shows plan details only when the API reports billing enabled.
projects.coreMechanism: Fixed-step WebCodecs export shared by the browser and a headless render worker
projects.shippedOutcome: Public editor with six templates and local H.264 MP4 export

projects.title: Arkhiv
projects.summary: A shared archive engine for print, audio and video collections. It keeps each original file as the bytes it arrived in and serves a catalogue you can read or download. I built the Go backend, the PostgreSQL model, the React reader and the release and backup tooling.
projects.description: Arkhiv runs several branded archives from one engine, including the Anarchist Zine Archive, Bill Nye TV and Democracy Now! TV. Each original is stored with its SHA-256 and checked again before it is served. Where a source gives no rights information, the archive records none instead of assigning a reuse license. I built the Go service, the PostgreSQL schema and migrations, the React reader with pdf.js, the reusable viewer package and the backup tooling. Some collections and recovery checks are still open.
projects.problem: Zines and broadcast recordings scattered across upload sites change, vanish or lose their context. An archive has to keep the exact file and say plainly what it does not know about it, including who holds the rights.
highlights: Stores the exact source response bytes beside parsed metadata, so search fields and normalized records can be rebuilt without refetching anything.
Checks each original's hash and size before serving it and uses the hash as the ETag. Downloads match the source byte for byte.
Ships engine releases as immutable container digests with checksum-locked additive migrations, and backs up with hard-linked snapshots. An unchanged collection snapshot added about 4 MB.
architecture: Raw source records live in PostgreSQL as bytes keyed by SHA-256, with parsed fields in JSONB. Editorial decisions are stored separately, so a source update never overwrites them. The cost is storage.
The print module takes the PDF library from the app that uses it. Poppler extracts text, OCR is a fallback, and a revoked or corrupt original takes its derived files down with it.
Missing rights fields stay missing and pass through the API as unknown. A collection whose terms allow only streaming from the source is locked to that mode in both the domain code and the database.
lessons: A failed backup experiment showed that Compose teardown could leave a one-off restore container running. Cleanup now removes containers only by exact project label and refuses live project names.
A restore that missed its 30-minute deadline stays recorded as a failure. A later run with a longer budget is reported separately and does not count as meeting the original target.
projects.coreMechanism: SHA-256 preservation of original bytes with per-read verification
projects.shippedOutcome: Public catalogue with an in-browser reader and byte-exact downloads

projects.title: Kork
projects.summary: A free link page for socials, tip buttons, music, video, QR codes and a contact card. Tips go straight to the owner's own accounts. I built the Go service, the server-rendered public pages, the React editor and the PostgreSQL model. It is new, so expect rough edges.
projects.description: Kork publishes one page per person at a short address. It supports 92 services and ten themes, renders public pages as plain HTML with a strict content security policy, and counts visits without storing IPs, cookies or user agents. I built the Go API and renderer, the embedded React editor, the URL validation and outbound fetching, the link screening and the analytics. Custom domains and paid plans exist in the code but are switched off on the public service.
projects.problem: Link-in-bio services are where creators put their tip links, and many of them take a cut, add trackers or route payments through themselves. Kork links to the owner's own payment accounts and never handles the money.
highlights: Defined each of the 92 services in code with its allowed hosts and handle pattern. Tests reject look-alike domains, javascript: links and URLs with credentials.
Built one outbound fetcher for link import, previews and latest-post feeds. It checks the resolved IP when the connection opens, which blocks DNS rebinding to internal addresses.
Counts page views as daily totals by referrer domain and country only, with no IPs, cookies or user agents stored.
architecture: One Go binary serves the API, the public pages and the embedded React editor. Public pages are server-rendered HTML with one small script and no third-party requests except embeds the owner adds.
New accounts wait 24 hours before publishing, and links are screened against a phishing list refreshed daily. The README states that the list cannot catch every threat.
Sessions use HttpOnly SameSite cookies, writes require a custom request header against CSRF, passwords use argon2id, and tokens are stored only as SHA-256 hashes.
lessons: Country counts trusted a forwarded header anyone could set. Without an explicit trusted-proxy setting, those views now count as unknown.

Public copy has to match what the code enforces. The README states the exact service count and that custom domains are off, and the confirmation notice no longer says a new account can publish right away.
projects.coreMechanism: Per-service URL validation and a rebinding-safe outbound fetcher
projects.shippedOutcome: Free public link pages with 92 services, ten themes and tracker-free analytics

projects.title: Backline
projects.summary: A Discord bot and dashboard for the people running a server: onboarding, moderation cases, private tickets, feeds and recovery snapshots, in 23 modules switched on per server. I built the bot, the Express API, the React dashboard and the backup tooling. It is in a private pilot, and public installation is not open.
projects.description: Backline started as Discord Spywatcher, a presence-analytics bot, and I rebuilt it in 2026 as a community tool. Every module starts disabled and is turned on per server. I built the discord.js bot and its durable job worker, the Express and Prisma API on PostgreSQL, Discord OAuth sign-in, the React dashboard and a backup script that proves each dump by restoring it. The pilot runs in a few approved servers. Public installation, global command registration and a sustained observation period are still to come.
projects.problem: Small Discord communities often run several bots for welcome roles, moderation, tickets and feeds, each with its own settings and records. Moderators need one case history, and owners need to switch features on only where they are wanted.
highlights: Made all 23 modules opt-in per server. The registry reads current settings on each event, so turning a module off takes effect without a restart.
Checks live Discord permissions on every configuration change. Sessions and API keys need the same current authorization as a fresh member fetch.
Verifies each nightly backup by restoring it into a disposable database and comparing every public table's rows and sequence values before keeping it.
architecture: Jobs are claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED under 30-second leases. When the outcome of a Discord action is uncertain, the job is held for reconciliation instead of retried, because Discord and PostgreSQL cannot commit one transaction together.
Closed ticket channels and their local transcripts expire after 1 to 90 days, even when the module is later switched off. Message content is left out of transcripts by default.
Discord rate limits are retried once when the reset is five seconds or less. Longer limits fail the request instead of holding a user's sign-in open.
lessons: Each check proves one thing. A restore receipt proves database rows and sequences match. It does not prove a Discord action or an OAuth flow, so the pilot notes list what is still unverified.
Duplicate side effects are worse than a stuck job. Recovery confirms the current state and never retries a create, overwrite or delete on its own.
projects.coreMechanism: Per-server module gates with live permission checks and reconciled durable jobs
projects.shippedOutcome: Private pilot of 23 community modules with restore-verified backups

projects.title: Jury-Rigged
projects.summary: A real-time courtroom simulation with agents playing the judge, attorneys, witnesses, and bailiff. Viewers can participate through Twitch chat commands.
projects.description: Court cases in Jury-Rigged move through deterministic phases while agents play the judge, prosecutor, defense, witnesses, and bailiff. The backend streams events over SSE, records sessions for replay, and supports jury voting and deliberation. A React operator dashboard controls case flow, while PixiJS renders proceedings for viewers.
projects.problem: A live courtroom simulation must keep unpredictable agent dialogue inside a reliable case sequence. It also needs to accept audience commands without letting chat derail the proceedings.
highlights: Built a multi-agent courtroom simulation with deterministic phase progression, live SSE streaming, and jury voting and deliberation mechanics.
Rendered proceedings in Ace Attorney visual style using PixiJS, with character animations, dialogue boxes, and courtroom transitions.
Integrated Twitch chat commands (!press, !objection) for real-time audience participation, plus NDJSON recording for deterministic session replay.
architecture: A Node.js, TypeScript and Express backend runs the agents through OpenRouter. Deterministic phase state machines decide where the case goes next.
A PixiJS layer draws the courtroom in an Ace Attorney style: character sprites, dialogue overlays and animated transitions, all driven by the agent output stream.
There are two interfaces: the viewer stream, rendered in PixiJS with Twitch chat wired in, and a React and Vite operator dashboard for case management and phase control.
lessons: Replaying NDJSON recordings was how I debugged agent behavior. Running the exact same sequence again, without LLM variance, made the multi-agent interactions much easier to tune.
Twitch commands such as !objection need to enter the same phase model as agent actions so audience input cannot bypass courtroom state.
projects.coreMechanism: Deterministic courtroom phase machine with SSE events and recorded replay
projects.shippedOutcome: Interactive courtroom simulation with operator and Twitch audience controls

projects.title: Patchwork
projects.summary: A mutual-aid development preview built on AT Protocol. I worked on public-record ingestion, neighborhood discovery, and approximate-location privacy. It is not approved for arranging real help.
projects.description: Mutual-aid discovery needs enough location data to connect nearby people, and no more. I designed Patchwork to reduce the coordinate precision of a request before it is stored, then built the React client, query API, Jetstream ingestion pipeline and moderation worker around that rule. Approved public resources are the exception and can show their addresses. The demonstration environment shows the record lifecycle, the location model and the moderation flow.
projects.problem: Storing the exact location of someone asking for help puts that person at risk. A request has to be findable by neighbors without recording where anyone lives.
highlights: Separated the React client, query API, ingestion pipeline, and moderation worker into independently testable workspaces with explicit contracts.
Reduced request location precision before persistence, so finding a request does not require storing or returning its exact coordinates.
Tested the record lifecycle, location boundaries, moderation flow and accessibility in the demonstration environment.
architecture: Because ingestion, moderation, querying, and presentation fail differently, I separated them into four workspaces with shared types. This isolates testing and deployment while preserving one TypeScript contract surface.
Bluesky Jetstream provides the external event stream, while PostgreSQL stores the indexed records and community metadata Patchwork needs to query independently of the upstream feed.
Location precision is reduced before persistence, not only hidden in the interface. That protects the storage and API boundaries but limits how precisely the map can rank nearby requests.
lessons: Using an external identity protocol reduces custom account code but does not remove authorization, moderation, or account-lifecycle responsibilities.
Location privacy has to be tested at every place a value can leak: what is stored, returned, logged and drawn on the map. Calling it a UI setting does not cover that.

projects.title: Augr
projects.summary: A trading system in active development. Agents analyze, argue the bull and bear cases and review risk before any order is placed, and a paper-trading mode tests the whole path without risking capital.
projects.description: Augr moves a trade through parallel analysis, bull and bear debate, signal generation, risk debate, and execution. Its Go backend connects multiple model providers, market-data feeds, and broker adapters. Operators can use a Cobra CLI, Bubble Tea TUI, REST API, WebSocket stream, or React dashboard. Paper trading tests the workflow against market data without risking capital.
projects.problem: A generated trade signal should not reach a broker before opposing analysis and risk review. The same pipeline also needs a paper-trading path for testing without capital risk.
highlights: Built a five-phase pipeline where analysts debate bull and bear cases and risk across multiple rounds before producing execution signals.
Built broker adapters for Alpaca and Binance with paper-trading modes, enabling full pipeline testing against real market data without capital risk.
Integrated six LLM providers and four market data sources behind unified interfaces, allowing runtime provider switching without pipeline changes.
architecture: A Go 1.25 backend runs five phases in order: parallel analysis, a three-round research debate, a trading signal, a three-round risk debate, and execution. Each phase emits structured output for the next.
One LLM interface covers OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter, XAI and Ollama. One market-data interface covers Alpha Vantage, Polygon, Yahoo Finance and Binance.
Operators get a Cobra CLI and a Bubble Tea TUI. A chi/v5 REST API with WebSocket streaming feeds the React and Vite dashboard, PostgreSQL 17 keeps state, and Redis 7 caches.
lessons: Giving agents opposing mandates (bull against bear, aggressive against conservative) and several rounds surfaced objections that a single-pass analysis did not raise.
A paper-trading adapter is only useful if it simulates latency, partial fills and slippage. A mock that always fills instantly makes a strategy look better than it is.
projects.coreMechanism: Five-phase analysis, debate, risk review, and broker execution pipeline
projects.shippedOutcome: Active-development trading system with CLI, TUI, dashboard, and paper trading

projects.title: Clustr/Clustr-Galaxy
projects.summary: A graph-analysis platform and controller-first Unity client that turn Reddit community relationships into an explorable, revision-pinned galaxy.
projects.description: Clustr maps relationships between Reddit communities and publishes them as revision-pinned graph data. A Go backend handles API serving, crawling, and graph precalculation; PostgreSQL stores nodes, edges, and community assignments; and React provides analytical 2D/3D views. Clustr Galaxy extends that system with a controller-first Unity client for exploring the published community universe as a flyable galaxy, using bounded API payloads, deterministic orbital models, discovery-gated surveying, and offline-safe fallbacks.
projects.problem: Reddit does not expose which communities cluster together, which ones bridge groups, or how those relationships change over time.
highlights: Built Clustr Galaxy as a Unity 6 client that pins immutable graph revisions and streams bounded overview, region, community, and entity payloads from the Clustr API.
Implemented Louvain community detection to identify clusters of related subreddits from crawled relationship data.
Built interactive 3D and 2D force-directed graph visualizations using WebGL, with dashboard views and drill-down into detected community clusters.
Added k6 load tests, security audits, performance profiles, and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring across the stack.
architecture: The Go backend separates API serving, subreddit crawling, and graph precalculation. Each service can be deployed and monitored on its own.
PostgreSQL stores subreddit nodes, relationship edges and precomputed community assignments, with sqlc generating type-safe queries.
The Vite and React frontend renders interactive WebGL force-directed graphs in 3D, 2D, dashboard, and community views.
lessons: Running Louvain detection on the full dataset in real time was too slow for interactive use. Precalculating it in batches fixed that, and the frontend stopped waiting on it.
Load testing with k6 early caught a connection pool exhaustion bug before real crawl traffic could find it for me.
projects.coreMechanism: Revision-pinned Reddit graphs with precomputed Louvain community assignments
projects.shippedOutcome: Live beta with web graph analysis and a controller-first Unity explorer

projects.title: Internet-ID
projects.summary: A content provenance system that records cryptographic hashes, IPFS manifests and on-chain ownership claims. The original file never has to be uploaded to a central platform.
projects.description: Internet-ID hashes a creator's content, signs a provenance manifest, stores metadata on IPFS, and anchors the claim through a Solidity registry contract. The original file does not need to go to a central platform. A web app, API, async worker, and browser extension let audiences verify claims where they find the content.
projects.problem: Creators need to prove when they claimed a work without handing the original to another centralized platform. Verification should also be available on the pages where audiences find that work.
highlights: Designed a content provenance pipeline: hash content, sign a manifest, pin to IPFS, and register the claim on-chain through a Solidity smart contract on L2.
Built a cross-browser extension (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) for one-click ownership verification directly on YouTube and Twitter pages.
Passed Slither security audits on the ContentRegistry smart contract and met WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards on the frontend.
architecture: The ContentRegistry contract is Solidity on an L2, built with Hardhat and TypeScript, integrated through Ethers v6 and checked with Slither static analysis.
The frontend is Next.js App Router with NextAuth. An Express API uses Prisma, a BullMQ queue handles IPFS pinning asynchronously, and Redis caches verification lookups.
The browser extension supports Chrome, Firefox and Safari. It injects the verification UI into YouTube and Twitter pages and talks to the API through cross-origin message passing.
lessons: IPFS pinning reliability varies a lot between providers. I put Infura, Web3.Storage and Pinata behind one interface with automatic failover.
Supporting three browser engines (Chromium, Gecko, WebKit) took more platform-specific code than I expected. A shared core with thin platform adapters is what worked.
projects.coreMechanism: Signed content hashes anchored by IPFS manifests and a Solidity registry
projects.shippedOutcome: Content provenance claims verified through a web app and browser extension

projects.title: SoundHash
projects.summary: An audio fingerprinting system that uses spectral analysis to match short clips against known recordings across social platforms.
projects.description: SoundHash uses STFT peak detection to turn video and audio into compact fingerprints. It compares those fingerprints with known recordings, including clips changed by compression, re-encoding, or trimming. A FastAPI service handles ingestion and matching, PostgreSQL stores fingerprints and metadata, and Twitter and Reddit bots can flag matches. JWT authentication, API docs, traffic protection, and email alerts support the service.
projects.problem: Exact file hashes fail after audio is compressed, re-encoded, or clipped. Cross-platform matching needs fingerprints that survive those changes.
highlights: Built an audio fingerprinting pipeline using STFT spectral analysis and peak detection, producing compact vectors robust to compression, re-encoding, and partial clips.
Integrated automated Twitter and Reddit bots that detect and flag matched audio content across social media platforms.
Added WAF and DDoS protection, threat detection, and email notifications for match alerts.
architecture: STFT spectral analysis extracts frequency peaks. Those are hashed into compact fingerprint vectors and stored in PostgreSQL for similarity matching.
A FastAPI REST API with JWT auth and Swagger/ReDoc docs fronts the pipeline: audio extraction from video, fingerprint generation and database matching.
A bot layer uses the Twitter and Reddit APIs to monitor content, with configurable matching thresholds and alert routing.
lessons: A fingerprint that survives re-encoding and compression catches more real-world matches than one tuned for exact-match accuracy.
Rate limits on the social media APIs shaped the bot architecture more than the audio processing did. Batching and backoff were what kept it running.
projects.coreMechanism: Spectral audio fingerprinting with resilient acoustic hash indexing
projects.shippedOutcome: Audio matching service with Twitter and Reddit monitoring

projects.title: Galdr
projects.summary: A customer health scoring platform that combines Stripe, HubSpot, and Intercom data into automated health scores for B2B SaaS teams.
projects.description: Galdr combines billing, CRM, and support signals from Stripe, HubSpot, and Intercom into customer health scores. A Go backend and React 19 frontend use PostgreSQL for persistence. Docker supports local and production environments, while a manual GitHub Actions workflow deploys to a VPS behind Nginx.
projects.problem: Billing, support, and engagement data live in separate systems. B2B SaaS teams need one account view instead of manually comparing Stripe, HubSpot, and Intercom records.
highlights: Built the scoring workflow that combines Stripe, HubSpot and Intercom data into one customer health score for B2B SaaS teams.
Shipped a full-stack implementation with a Go net/http API, React 19 + TypeScript frontend, PostgreSQL 16 persistence, and Docker-based dev/prod workflows.
Added manual GitHub Actions deployment to a VPS behind Nginx, frontend SEO artifact generation, and a separate Stripe billing domain.
architecture: Go backend organized around internal handler, middleware, model, repository, and service layers, with migrations managing the PostgreSQL 16 data model.
React 19 + TypeScript frontend built with Vite and TailwindCSS v4, including SEO validation, sitemap artifact generation, and prerender steps in the frontend build pipeline.
Containerized development and production topology using Docker Compose, Nginx, and a manual GitHub Actions deploy workflow that targets a VPS and verifies both database readiness and API health.
lessons: Billing lives in its own domain, with dedicated Stripe endpoints and its own environment contract. That kept payment code out of the scoring flows.
Validating SEO artifacts during the build catches missing public metadata before deployment. A scripted VPS path also removes manual server-side deployment steps.
projects.coreMechanism: Customer health scoring from Stripe, HubSpot, and Intercom signals
projects.shippedOutcome: B2B customer health dashboard backed by Go and PostgreSQL

projects.title: Cutroom
projects.summary: A short-form video production system where specialized agents claim stages in a seven-step workflow from research through publishing.
projects.description: Cutroom moves a short video through seven stages from research to publishing. A specialized agent can claim each stage, and every handoff uses structured output. The Next.js 14 and React 18 dashboard connects to Prisma and PostgreSQL, Remotion rendering, ElevenLabs voice generation, Pexels visuals, and attribution on Base. The hosted app includes templates, pipeline views, and examples.
projects.problem: Research, scripting, voice, visuals, editing, and publishing produce different artifacts. Cutroom gives each stage a defined handoff so the next worker does not have to reconstruct earlier decisions.
highlights: Built a seven-stage production pipeline that turns a topic into a short-form video through structured handoffs.
Shipped a template-driven creative system with real-time pipeline tracking, attribution weights, and token-based reward logic for contributors.
Integrated Remotion rendering, ElevenLabs voice synthesis, and multi-platform publishing workflows behind a single hosted dashboard.
architecture: Next.js 14 app-router frontend and API surface share a TypeScript codebase, with dashboard pages, REST endpoints, and pipeline orchestration living in the same application boundary.
Prisma-backed PostgreSQL persistence stores pipelines, stages, and attribution metadata while Remotion assembles the final video output from structured stage artifacts.
External integrations connect voice generation, visual sourcing, and Base token distribution so the production flow can move from topic intake to published asset without ad hoc handoff glue.
lessons: Handoff structure mattered more than model quality here: the clearer the schema between stages, the less rework the editing stage had to absorb.
Attribution changes the data model because every stage must retain its contributor and weight. Adding it after rendering would lose that history.
projects.coreMechanism: Seven-stage production workflow with structured agent handoffs and Remotion rendering
projects.shippedOutcome: Hosted short-form video workflow with templates and pipeline tracking

projects.title: Subcults
projects.summary: An active-development platform for underground music scenes with coarse-location map discovery and live audio, without algorithmic feeds.
projects.description: Subcults maps underground music scenes, events, and live audio sessions without ranking them through a follower feed. A Go API and Jetstream indexer support a React and MapLibre frontend. PostGIS stores spatial data, LiveKit runs audio sessions, Cloudflare R2 stores media, and Stripe Connect handles direct scene payouts. Coarse-location controls limit what discovery reveals.
projects.problem: Underground scenes need discovery and coordination tools without giving up control or publishing precise locations. A ranked social feed works against both needs.
highlights: Designed a scene-first platform for underground music communities with map-based discovery, scene identity, and privacy-aware event publishing.
Combined AT Protocol Jetstream ingestion, live audio sessions and direct payout tooling in one product that has no algorithmic feed.
Added coarse-location controls, EXIF stripping, observability, security scanning, and privacy documentation early in development.
architecture: Go API and Jetstream indexer handle core application flows plus decentralized AT Protocol ingestion, with Neon Postgres 16 + PostGIS storing spatial and trust-aware community data.
Vite + React + TypeScript frontend uses MapLibre for scene and event discovery, while LiveKit powers real-time audio rooms and Cloudflare R2 stores media assets and recordings.
Docker Compose runs the API, indexer, and frontend behind an external reverse proxy. The workflow also checks metrics, vulnerabilities, and performance budgets.
lessons: Making precise location optional and consent-based forced the map and discovery flows to be explicit about what they show. The product is clearer for it.
Governance and observability had to arrive as early as the discovery features. For an underground scene, trust and safety are part of the product.
projects.coreMechanism: Jetstream scene indexing with PostGIS discovery and LiveKit audio sessions
projects.shippedOutcome: Active-development home for privacy-aware scene, event, and live audio discovery

projects.title: Llama Line
projects.summary: A Go HTTP broker that serializes Ollama inference through a visible FIFO queue, streaming live wait-time updates so users can see their position.
projects.description: Llama Line is a Go HTTP broker for Ollama. A strict FIFO queue allows one inference request at a time across generate, chat, embed, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. SSE reports queue position and elapsed wait, while non-inference routes pass through immediately. The broker handles disconnects, retries Ollama outages with backoff, layers YAML, environment, and CLI config, and exposes a public health endpoint.
projects.problem: Concurrent requests compete for one local GPU, but Ollama clients cannot see that contention. Users need to know their queue position and how long they have waited.
highlights: Built a strict FIFO broker that keeps only one Ollama inference request active at a time while preserving immediate passthrough for non-inference routes.
Streamed live queue position and elapsed wait updates over SSE so clients can track broker progress without polling.
Added resilient retry and backoff handling for Ollama outages plus YAML, env, and CLI configuration overrides for local AI deployments.
architecture: Go HTTP gateway serializes inference requests across Ollama endpoints, with a single in-flight job at a time and immediate proxying for non-inference traffic.
SSE status stream reports queue position and elapsed wait time while the broker tracks disconnects and recovers from upstream availability issues with retry/backoff.
YAML configuration is layered with environment and CLI overrides, static API-key auth secures the broker, and /broker/status remains unauthenticated for health checks.
lessons: One GPU means waiting. A visible FIFO queue makes that wait explainable; without it, contention just looks like a hang.
Because the broker speaks the Ollama API, existing tools need little more than a new address to use it.
projects.coreMechanism: Strict FIFO Ollama broker with one in-flight inference request and SSE wait updates
projects.shippedOutcome: Ollama-compatible gateway with visible GPU backpressure

projects.title: Open Pilot
projects.summary: A self-hosted automation service that turns approved Gitea issues into tested pull requests through OpenCode-driven code changes in isolated worktrees.
projects.description: Open Pilot turns approved Gitea issues into OpenCode jobs. A webhook adds ready issues to a durable queue. One worker claims each job, creates a git worktree, edits the code, runs tests, and pushes a branch for a pull request. Logging, a dashboard, a scheduler, and supervisor helpers are available, but the optional services stay disabled by default.
projects.problem: Issue-driven code automation can change and push a repository, so operators need a clear approval boundary, isolated worktrees, test results, and durable job logs.
highlights: Built the issue-to-PR runner that receives ready issue webhooks, claims jobs from a durable queue, and drives OpenCode changes inside a git worktree.
Added conservative self-hosted defaults with FIFO ordering, a single worker, and dashboard and scheduler features disabled unless explicitly turned on.
Integrated test execution, branch pushing, logging and helper services around that runner.
architecture: Webhook receiver accepts ready issue events from Gitea and places them into a durable queue backed by SQLite.
A single worker claims queued jobs, uses OpenCode in a dedicated worktree, runs tests, and pushes the result as a branch or pull request.
Dashboard, scheduler, supervisor and autopilot helpers exist but stay opt-in. The default install is a small MVP for a trusted, self-hosted setup.
lessons: Trusted automation still needs conservative defaults; FIFO scheduling and one-worker execution make the first self-hosted deployment easier to reason about.
In an issue-to-PR system, policy, logs, tests and worktree isolation are the product, and I treat them that way.
projects.coreMechanism: Durable Gitea issue queue with one OpenCode worker per isolated git worktree
projects.shippedOutcome: Self-hosted issue-to-PR automation with tests and operator logs

projects.title: Edda
projects.summary: An LLM-powered dungeon master application in Go that serves both a terminal UI and REST API from the same game logic.
projects.description: Edda runs an LLM-powered game master through either a terminal UI or REST API. The cmd/tui and cmd/server entry points share game logic from internal packages, while pkg/api exports integration types. Koanf reads YAML and GM_ environment variables, goose manages database migrations, and Docker Compose runs the local stack.
projects.problem: A game master needs an interactive interface, while integrations need an API. Both should use the same rules and state instead of duplicating game logic.
highlights: Built a Go application that serves both a terminal game-master experience and a REST API from the same codebase.
Structured the project around cmd/tui and cmd/server entry points, internal packages, and exported pkg/api types for external integration.
Added YAML and GM_-prefixed env configuration, goose migrations, and Docker Compose support for repeatable local deployment.
architecture: Go runtime splits into TUI and server entry points so interactive play and API access share the same game logic.
Koanf layers YAML and GM_ environment variables into one config surface, while goose manages schema changes for the Postgres-backed game state.
Docker Compose provides a reproducible local stack for the app, API, and database.
lessons: People want a terminal and integrations want an API. Separate entry points over shared game logic serve both without duplicating the rules.
Boring infrastructure helped. With explicit migrations, layered config and repeatable containers, the model was one of the few moving parts left to debug.
projects.coreMechanism: Shared Go game logic behind separate terminal and REST API entry points
projects.shippedOutcome: LLM game master available through a TUI and REST API

projects.title: Paqr
projects.summary: A research data packager that turns messy datasets into documented, searchable HDF5 archives with provenance tracking and mock-first defaults.
projects.description: Paqr scans research folders, normalizes names, paths, and tables, records schema and provenance, and packages the result as HDF5. A searchable inventory is available through a REST API, CLI, Streamlit browser, and React shell. Docker Compose runs the app with PostgreSQL, and AI_MODE=mock keeps local development independent of external model providers.
projects.problem: Research folders mix formats, naming rules, and incomplete metadata. Packaging them without recording each transformation makes the resulting archive hard to trust.
highlights: Built a pipeline that discovers messy research folders, sanitizes names and tabular data, and packages the result into documented HDF5 archives.
Shipped a searchable inventory plus REST API and CLI commands for scanning, profiling, packaging, searching, and serving research datasets.
Added a Streamlit browser, React frontend shell, PostgreSQL-backed persistence, and mock-first AI defaults for safe local use.
architecture: Discovery and sanitization stages normalize file paths and tabular content before metadata extraction records schema and provenance.
A packaging step emits HDF5 artifacts and indexed inventory data exposed through FastAPI and CLI entry points.
The app runs with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL, while the UI stack combines Streamlit browsing with a React shell.
lessons: A research package should record provenance during each transformation. Reconstructing it afterward leaves gaps.
Mock-first AI defaults make data tooling easier to demo, test, and trust before connecting it to external model providers.
projects.coreMechanism: Dataset discovery, sanitization, provenance capture, and HDF5 packaging pipeline
projects.shippedOutcome: Searchable research archive with CLI, REST, and Streamlit access

projects.title: Redstring
projects.summary: A design-stage litigation workspace concept that organizes documents, filings, facts, and deadlines into a structured case graph for legal teams.
projects.description: Redstring is a litigation workspace concept for paralegals and lawyers. Its case graph links documents, filings, deadlines, communications, and facts so teams can track what is known, disputed, or awaiting follow-up. Docker and Make provide a repeatable local foundation for the workspace.
projects.problem: Legal evidence is split across documents, filings, and communications. Folder trees do not capture which facts support or conflict with each other.
highlights: Modeled legal work around evidence, facts, deadlines, and communications instead of a flat document dump.
Set up a Docker-based local foundation for testing the case workspace with its supporting services.
Designed suggested facts to retain source links so a legal reviewer could trace their provenance.
architecture: Dockerized application stack with service boundaries for the case workspace, persistence layer, and supporting local infrastructure.
Data model centers documents, filings, deadlines, communications, and extracted facts so attorneys can navigate from evidence to argument.
The searchable workspace keeps case context linked to source material rather than detached summaries.
lessons: A legal reviewer has to be able to trace every suggested fact back to its source, so provenance comes first in the interface.
Legal work is mostly relationships between facts, filings and evidence. A graph models that better than a folder tree.
projects.coreMechanism: Case graph linking evidence, facts, filings, deadlines, and communications
projects.shippedOutcome: Foundation for a traceable litigation case workspace

projects.title: Switchyard
projects.summary: An automation runtime in active development. It routes workflow state between services and shows operators where each piece of work is.
projects.description: Switchyard is an active-development automation runtime. Its Go backend routes workflow state, while a Vite, React, and TypeScript interface lets operators inspect work and service handoffs. The Dockerized monorepo provides the current foundation for adding workflow modules.
projects.problem: Background automation is difficult to operate when queues and handoffs appear only in logs. Operators need to inspect routed work and its current state.
highlights: Built a full-stack automation runtime foundation with Go services and a Vite React operator interface.
Added Make and Docker workflows for running the Go and React services together.
Focused the product around visible workflow routing instead of opaque background scripts.
architecture: Go backend exposes workflow and runtime primitives while the React frontend provides an operator-facing control surface.
Docker Compose and Make targets run local development and tests across the backend and frontend.
Runtime model treats automation as routed work with inspectable state, making failures and handoffs easier to reason about.
lessons: When queues, decisions and handoff state are on screen, a failed handoff is something an operator can find. In log-only automation it is something they reconstruct.
projects.coreMechanism: Routed workflow state exposed by a Go runtime and React operator interface
projects.shippedOutcome: Active-development foundation for visible workflow routing and handoffs

projects.title: Subcult OS
projects.summary: Software in development for running a show night: free ticket reservations, staffing, door check-in, security logs, vendor payout calculations and night-close reconciliation.
projects.description: Subcult OS covers free ticket reservations, door scanning, staff scheduling, security incident logs, vendor payout calculations and night-close reports for an event. I built the foundation with a Go backend, a Vite and React frontend, and PostgreSQL. It is still in development.
projects.problem: Live event work is split across spreadsheets, ticketing systems, staff rosters and cash records. I am building Subcult OS to keep admissions, incidents, shifts, settlements and closing reports in the same system.
highlights: Built event workflows covering free ticket reservations, door check-in and guest lists.
Created operational modules for staff shift scheduling, security incident logging, and automated vendor payout calculations.
Designed financial tracking and night-close reports for door revenue, bar cuts, and vendor disbursements.
architecture: Go API and Vite React frontend run as separate services against a Postgres persistence layer with transactional event state management.
Door and security check-in screens target quick use on phones and tablets under poor venue connectivity.
Closing reports combine admission counts, vendor receipts, and staff hours.
lessons: On the night, the door screen has to be fast and has to survive bad venue connectivity. A multi-step flow loses to that every time.
Night-close reports need source records for admissions, receipts, and staff hours so discrepancies can be traced.
projects.coreMechanism: Event lifecycle state spanning ticketing, door scanning, vendor settlement, and night-close reconciliation
projects.shippedOutcome: Active-development foundation for live-event operations and night-close reporting

projects.title: Subcult.tv
projects.summary: The Subculture Collective's public catalog of projects, tools, media, and infrastructure for independent digital culture.
projects.description: Subcult.tv gives the Subculture Collective one public home for its identity, project catalog, tools, and media. The TypeScript site uses Docker and Make for local and deployment workflows.
projects.problem: The collective's work spans many repositories. Without a maintained public index, visitors lose the context connecting those projects.
highlights: Built SUBCULT's public catalog across projects, tools, media, and infrastructure.
Packaged the site with Docker and Make workflows used by the collective's other services.
Created a catalog-style entry point for the collective rather than scattering project context across repos.
architecture: The TypeScript web application keeps public pages, project content and the collective's own description in one repository.
Dockerized deployment keeps the public site aligned with the operational pattern used by other SUBCULT services.
The content model links projects, tools, and infrastructure in one catalog.
lessons: Without a maintained index, the context connecting the collective's projects ends up scattered across repositories.
The public site is easier to maintain when it builds and deploys the same way as the application code.

media.alt: Subcult.tv home presenting open-source tools for independent culture and links to selected work and field notes.
media.caption: Public Subcult.tv home captured after the focused positioning and navigation pass.

projects.coreMechanism: TypeScript content catalog for the collective's projects, tools, and media
projects.shippedOutcome: Public home and project index for the Subculture Collective

projects.title: Invisible Museum
projects.summary: A place-based museum prototype pairing a SwiftUI iOS app with a Go backend, letting physical locations host lightweight exhibits and stories.
projects.description: Invisible Museum is a place-based museum prototype. A SwiftUI iOS app reads lightweight exhibits, stories, and artifacts tied to physical locations from a Dockerized Go and PostgreSQL backend.
projects.problem: Stories about a place often lose context inside a general archive or feed. A location-aware exhibit can present them where they happened.
highlights: Built a SwiftUI prototype for discovering exhibits tied to real-world locations.
Added a Dockerized Go/PostgreSQL backend so place metadata and exhibit content can be served locally.
Explored museum UX as a location-aware layer instead of a conventional archive or gallery feed.
architecture: SwiftUI client handles the mobile exhibit experience while a Go backend exposes location and exhibit APIs.
PostgreSQL stores places, exhibit records, and supporting metadata for local development and deployment.
Dockerized backend makes it possible to test the mobile experience against a realistic service instead of mocks.
lessons: Someone using this is already walking, so the mobile screen has to be small and fast.
Attaching exhibits to places turns the data model around: the place comes first and the collection second.
projects.coreMechanism: SwiftUI location-based exhibits served by a Go and PostgreSQL backend
projects.shippedOutcome: Prototype for discovering museum stories at physical locations

projects.title: Echo Trails
projects.summary: A concept foundation for short stories tied to real-world locations and discovered in context.
projects.description: Echo Trails is a concept for short public stories tied to real-world places. People leave an echo at a location, and others discover it in context. The foundation centers place records, lightweight story capture, and local discovery.
projects.problem: Place-based stories lose their setting in a global social feed. Capturing one should also take less effort than publishing a full post.
highlights: Designed a place-story model around short public echoes attached to real locations.
Framed the product around contextual discovery rather than social-feed consumption.
Kept the concept foundation small, with Make commands for repeatable local work.
architecture: Place records anchor the product model, with story entries attached to physical locations.
Frontend discovery surfaces prioritize nearby/contextual reading over global ranking.
The prototype uses Make commands for repeatable local development.
lessons: If leaving a story feels like publishing a post, most people will not do it. Capture has to be quick.
A local discovery product should be judged on context and memory. Time spent scrolling is the wrong measure.
projects.coreMechanism: Short public story records attached to physical places
projects.shippedOutcome: Concept foundation for capturing and discovering local stories

projects.title: Nearbody
projects.summary: A phone-based body-doubling concept: quick shared presence for someone who knows what the task is and cannot get started on it.
projects.description: Nearbody is a phone-based body-doubling concept for starting hard tasks. It focuses on quick shared presence and one task-start moment instead of backlogs, plans, and other productivity features.
projects.problem: People avoiding a known task often need help starting, not another planning system. Joining a body-doubling session must take little setup.
highlights: Defined a task-starting product around body doubling rather than task management.
Focused the UX on immediate phone-based presence and activation support.
Kept the prototype narrow: help the user begin one hard thing instead of managing a full backlog.
architecture: Product model centers sessions, participants, and the task-start moment rather than large project/task hierarchies.
The mobile interface keeps joining steps and setup short.
The concept foundation leaves real-time presence and notifications for later work.
lessons: For task avoidance, the first minute is the product. Setup has to go before any management feature comes in.
Presence can be more motivating than planning when the user already knows what they need to do.
projects.coreMechanism: Phone-based body-doubling sessions centered on one task-start moment
projects.shippedOutcome: Narrow product concept for shared presence while starting a task

projects.title: One-Block Cinema
projects.summary: A smartphone filmmaking coach concept that turns one city block into a guided idea and shot plan for a short film.
projects.description: One-Block Cinema is a smartphone filmmaking coach concept for beginners and hobbyists. It guides a user from an idea to a shot list for a 1–3 minute film made within one city block. The workflow favors prompts and checklists over a blank editor.
projects.problem: A blank video editor does not help a beginner decide what to film. Limiting the shoot to one block and 1–3 minutes makes the first project manageable.
highlights: Created a guided filmmaking concept that converts everyday surroundings into short-film prompts.
Structured the planning flow around beginner-friendly idea prompts and shot lists.
Positioned the app as a creative coach rather than a generic video editor.
architecture: Workflow model breaks filmmaking into small stages suitable for phone-based creation.
Frontend experience emphasizes prompts, checklists, and shot guidance over complex editing controls.
The current foundation leaves capture and editing for a later mobile or web implementation.
lessons: Creative tools for beginners need constraints; narrowing to one block and 1–3 minutes makes the act of starting less intimidating.
Someone still learning the craft gets more from a coach than from a blank canvas.
projects.coreMechanism: Guided idea prompts and shot planning for a one-block film
projects.shippedOutcome: Planning concept for a guided idea and shot list for a 1–3 minute film

projects.title: Pocket Civilization
projects.summary: A passive lifelog simulation concept that turns personal traces into a small evolving civilization while keeping privacy controls explicit and local.
projects.description: Pocket Civilization is a passive lifelog simulation concept. It turns personal traces into a small evolving world while keeping privacy controls local and explicit. The current foundation includes privacy-control UI and models for memories, signals, and simulation state.
projects.problem: A lifelog can collect sensitive data before a user understands what the product derives from it. Signal-level consent and local controls need to exist before ingestion expands.
highlights: Explored a lifelog simulator where personal signals become a miniature evolving civilization.
Built privacy-control UI as an early product surface rather than a late settings page.
Framed simulation data around local control so sensitive traces do not become default cloud exhaust.
architecture: Simulation model separates raw personal traces from derived world state and user-facing civilization events.
Privacy-control interface governs what signals can enter the simulator and what remains local.
The current foundation leaves ingestion, timeline, and visualization modules for later work.
lessons: Lifelog products should begin with privacy controls because retrofitting consent after ingestion is too late.
Personal data feels less extractive when it turns into something playful that stays on the device. A dashboard of the same data reads as surveillance.
projects.coreMechanism: Privacy controls separating personal traces from derived civilization state
projects.shippedOutcome: Concept foundation and privacy UI for a local lifelog simulation

projects.title: PatrickFanella.co
projects.summary: This site: a React frontend, a Go API and a PostgreSQL content model, with repeatable deployment and verification.
projects.description: PatrickFanella.co runs this portfolio through a React frontend, Go API, and PostgreSQL content model. The repository includes migrations, seed data, a generated sitemap, and deployment documentation.
projects.problem: A portfolio could be a handful of static pages. I wanted the project data validated and reusable, so it got a schema, a seed file and a deployment path. That is more machinery than a portfolio strictly needs.
highlights: Built the public React interface and Go API around a PostgreSQL portfolio model.
Added migrations and seed validation so content changes follow the database schema.
Generated the sitemap from project content and documented the deployment path.
architecture: The React app reads portfolio data through a Go REST API.
PostgreSQL stores project records, with migrations and seed data defining content changes.
Docker supports local services and deployment, while prerendering supplies public pages and SEO metadata.
lessons: Keeping portfolio content in a schema catches missing fields and broken relationships before deployment.
Sitemap and prerender checks need to read the same records as the UI or public metadata will drift.
projects.coreMechanism: Go REST API, containerized PostgreSQL, and prerendered React SPA
projects.shippedOutcome: Production portfolio with axe, keyboard and Lighthouse checks in the release gate

projects.title: Artemis
projects.summary: An early TypeScript information site and API with repository automation. No product-specific behavior is defined yet.
projects.description: The repository contains a TypeScript information site, an API, and automation for repository changes. It does not yet define product-specific behavior.
projects.problem: No product-specific behavior is defined yet.
highlights: Set up the TypeScript information site and API.
Added repository automation.
architecture: The repository contains a TypeScript information site and API.
lessons: Repository automation can support changes before product-specific behavior is defined.
projects.coreMechanism: TypeScript information site and API
projects.shippedOutcome: Repository setup for a TypeScript information site, API, and automation

projects.title: Blacktower
projects.summary: My OpenCode setup, trimmed: a small set of agent roles, managed skills and workflow defaults that use fewer tokens.
projects.description: Blacktower packages my OpenCode configuration, selected agent roles, managed skills, and lower-token workflow defaults for daily coding work.
projects.problem: A large set of overlapping agent roles and verbose defaults wastes context and makes dispatch unpredictable. Blacktower keeps the roles and workflows I use in one configuration.
highlights: Curated agent roles around distinct implementation, research, and review jobs.
Set lower-token defaults for routine coding workflows.
Packaged managed skills and tool wiring with the OpenCode configuration.
architecture: OpenCode configuration registers the selected agents, tools, and managed skills.
Workflow defaults reduce context use for routine tasks.
Role boundaries separate implementation from research and review.
lessons: More agent roles do not improve routing when their responsibilities overlap.
Token limits work best as workflow defaults rather than reminders in every prompt.
projects.coreMechanism: OpenCode configuration wiring selected agent roles, tools, skills, and workflow defaults
projects.shippedOutcome: Curated coding toolkit with lower-token defaults and role-based dispatch

projects.title: tmux-popups
projects.summary: A tmux popup toolkit with a TSV registry, generated bindings, quick menu, local overrides, and diagnostics.
projects.description: Tmux Popups reads a TSV registry to generate popup bindings and a quick menu. Local overrides and diagnostics keep project-specific changes separate from the shared registry.
projects.problem: Hand-maintained tmux popup bindings drift across machines and projects. One registry should drive both bindings and the menu.

projects.title: Super Productivity MCP
projects.summary: Connect an AI client to a local task manager through a Go MCP server, in-app plugin, and desktop quick-add. A shared catalog keeps tool definitions, documentation, and bridge behavior aligned.
projects.description: Super Productivity MCP connects assisted planning to a local task system through a typed MCP interface, a Super Productivity plugin, and a native desktop quick-add path. Read and write actions stay explicit. Generated contract docs, protocol smoke tests, and package checks verify each release before installation.
projects.problem: Task automation must distinguish reads from mutations and work with the task manager already on the desktop. A prompt-only contract cannot enforce either requirement.
highlights: Built a Go MCP server and Super Productivity plugin connected through local file-based IPC.
Added desktop quick-add through the same plugin bridge, with explicit read/write and preview/confirmation boundaries.
Added release checks for catalog consistency, generated documentation, Go and JavaScript tests, protocol scenarios, installation profiles, and plugin packaging.
architecture: A Go MCP server and desktop quick-add client send requests to the in-app JavaScript plugin through inbox/outbox files. The plugin bridge must be running for either client to reach task data.
An installable plugin and desktop quick-add bridge provide two user-facing capture paths without requiring a hosted intermediary.
Generated catalogs, smoke tests, evaluation scenarios, and a reproducible packaging target keep documentation and shipped behavior aligned.
lessons: Agent integrations are safer when mutation boundaries are visible in the tool contract instead of being left to prompt convention.
Treating installation profiles and generated documentation as release artifacts prevents a passing unit suite from masking a broken user setup.

projects.title: VOD Tender
projects.summary: A service that finds and downloads public Twitch VODs and captures their chat logs for archival.

projects.title: Tadooer
projects.summary: A self-hosted task, calendar, and focus planner for one owner. The engineering work centers on queued task edits, explicit sync conflicts, CalDAV integration, and a focus session shared across clients.
projects.description: Tadooer puts tasks beside calendar events and one active focus session. The server is authoritative; browser task edits can queue temporarily offline and replay when connected. Calendar and focus commands need a connection. It is a private single-owner planner with public source, not a hosted signup service. Desktop and mobile shells have separate platform qualification requirements.
projects.problem: A planner used from several clients needs to survive a dropped connection without silently overwriting a calendar edit or starting competing focus sessions.
highlights: Built browser-local task caching and queued writes with replay protection and explicit two-client conflicts.
Integrated calendar planning through CalDAV with ETag-based conflict checks, alongside Google calendar projections with visible freshness.
Made focus sessions server-authoritative with one controller, read-only followers, and explicit takeover.
architecture: IndexedDB holds the browser task cache and immutable outbox. Foreground sync replays core task changes; calendar and focus mutations remain online-only.
Calendar changes use the previously observed DAV ETag. A concurrent edit becomes a conflict for the owner to resolve rather than an unconditional overwrite.
Web and desktop clients use the same server authority. A second client follows the active focus session until the owner explicitly takes control.
lessons: Offline support needs a command-by-command boundary. Queuing task edits is useful without pretending calendar or focus commands can run disconnected.
Conflict and freshness states belong in the planner interface, where the owner can make the decision.
